The new task reads bit 1 of each stimulus. Every assignment that fits says yellow when exactly one or both stimuli have a 1 there. The assignments disagree only on the six inputs where both bits are 0: red or yellow. A consistency pattern favours red, so the answer is not fully determined.

**Y components (which bit each one reads).** In every known task, one bit position separates the two buttons cleanly.

| Component | Bit | Evidence |
|---|---|---|
| Y4 | bit 2 | Task X2-Y4-Z3 gives green exactly when bit 2 is the same in both stimuli (all 24 examples). |
| Y2 | bit 3 | Task X2-Y2-Z1 gives red exactly when bit 3 is the same (all 24). |
| Y3 | bit 1 | Task X2-Y3-Z4 gives yellow exactly when bit 1 is the same (all 24). |
| Y1 | bit 4 | Task X5-Y1-Z3 gives yellow exactly when bit 4 is 1 in both stimuli (all 24). |

**X and Z components.** Two groups of assignments fit all six known tasks.

| Component | Version A | Version B |
|---|---|---|
| X2 | both are the same | exactly one is 1 |
| X5 | not both are 1 | both are 1 |
| Z1 | true → red | true → yellow |
| Z3 | true → green | true → yellow |
| Z4 | true → yellow | true → green |

- X5 is linked to X2 and Z4 through task X5-Y4-Z4, where green appears exactly when bit 2 is 1 in both stimuli. That is why X5 switches with the group.
- X4 is separate. Task X4-Y2-Z2 gives yellow exactly when neither stimulus has bit 3 set. So X4 is either "neither is 1" (with Z2 true → yellow) or "at least one is 1" (with Z2 true → blue). Either choice combines with A or B.

That gives four fitting assignments for X4-Y3-Z1:

- **A with "neither":** neither → red.
- **A with "at least one":** neither → yellow.
- **B with "neither":** neither → yellow.
- **B with "at least one":** neither → red.

**Pattern across components.** Group A's rules are all negated forms ("same" is not-exactly-one; "not both"). Group B's rules are all plain forms ("exactly one"; "both"). If X4 follows the same style, A pairs with "neither" and B with "at least one". Both of those pairings predict that "neither stimulus has bit 1 set" gives red. The other two assignments still fit, so the answers are not determined.

**Prediction:** red when bit 1 is 0 in both stimuli, otherwise yellow.

| # | Input | Bit 1 (stim 1, stim 2) | Button |
|---|---|---|---|
| 1 | 0000 0011 | 0, 0 | red |
| 2 | 0100 1111 | 0, 1 | yellow |
| 3 | 1001 1000 | 1, 1 | yellow |
| 4 | 0100 1000 | 0, 1 | yellow |
| 5 | 0011 0011 | 0, 0 | red |

| 8 | 1101 1110 | 1, 1 | yellow |

| 11 | 1111 0000 | 1, 0 | yellow |
| 12 | 0001 1010 | 0, 1 | yellow |
| 13 | 1101 0100 | 1, 0 | yellow |
| 14 | 0101 0000 | 0, 0 | red |

My confidence of 0.65 is roughly how much I trust the negated-versus-plain pattern; if it doesn't hold, the six red answers would all be yellow.

# Learn tasks from examples

Each task maps an input to one of four buttons: yellow, blue, red, or green. An input is a pair of stimuli; each stimulus has 4 binary features, written as 4 bits (bit positions 1-4, left to right). The line `1011 0110 -> red` means: stimulus 1 is 1011, stimulus 2 is 0110, and the correct button is red.

Every task is built from three components. A **Y component** picks one of the 4 features (bit positions 1-4); the task looks at that feature in both stimuli. An **X component** is a rule on those two bits, one of: both are 1; at least one is 1; exactly one is 1; neither is 1; not both are 1; both are the same. A **Z component** gives one button when the rule is true and a different button when it is false. A task's label lists its components, for example X2-Y1-Z3. Each kind has several versions (X1, X2, and so on); different versions of a kind are different from each other, and the same label always means the same component. You are not told which version does what.
